subject: combining predict and ranef to estimate density

messages.author: 0c8e4d9395a2aae5
messages.subject: combining predict and ranef to estimate density
parts:
Hello Unmarked Users,
 
I would like to estimate density of several species of forest songbirds in twelve ~50 ha forest stands, each of which contain at least ten point count stations.  I have 5 yrs. of post-treatment data and two surveys per year.  I have stacked data so that there are 126 stations x 5 yrs = 630 total rows of data.  I used Year as a covariate in all models.  Each stand has an additional 20 or so plots where we sampled habitat characteristics, but not birds.
 
So to estimate abundance I used the best gmultmix model for a species, and used "ranef" for plots we surveyed for both birds and habitat and "predict" for plots where we have only habitat data.  Dorazio et al. (2013) did something like this, though I'm not sure if I'm actually duplicating their procedure.  Also Kery et al. (2005) and Royle (2004) both used or advocated Laird & Louis's (1987) empirical Bayes confidence intervals based on bootstrap samples.  I think this is what function Ranef does, but I'm not sure.  I don't understand this function very well and I'm not sure if I'm interpreting these sources correctly. 
 
To get density I multiplied the abundance estimate for each station by the predicted availability and divided by the area of the point count (based on Chandler et al. 2011).  I then took the mean across point counts within a stand and year to get density at the stand/year level.  And then used the quantiles from the bootstrap output to get the confidence intervals. 
 
Does anyone see any problems with this approach?  Perhaps I should be using only ranef and the plots with bird data?  Am I accounting for enough variability using this bootstrap procedure?   
 
Here's an example model and my preliminary script for getting the abundance estimate and the bootstrap confidence interval.  Also a few lines of the output.  I really appreciate any thoughts on this.
 
Best,
 
Mike Worland
Wisconsin DNR
 
 
 
(mod<-
global<- gmultmix(~block +year +cnpyCV +ba +scDiv +dbh +con +yb,
                             ~block +year +dayDiff,
                             ~obsvr +sky +windy +time +date +ba +sap, uf))
#
# Bootstrap function. Uses "predict" to estimate abundance for non-surveyed plots
# that have only habitat data; uses "ranef" to estimate abundance for plots that
# have both bird and habitat data. Also uses predict to estimate availability (phi).
# Abundance needs to be multiplied by availability & divided by area to calculate
# density.
#
Nhat <- function(mod) {
  ab <-bup(ranef(mod))
  ab<- cbind(ab,xplot[,c(1,2,4,10)])
  phi <-predict (mod, xplot, type ="phi", append=T)
  abNB<- predict(mod, habNB, type="lambda", append=T)
  phiNB <-predict (mod, habNB, type ="phi", append=T)
  names(ab)[names(ab) =="ab"] <-"abund"
  names(phi)[names(phi) =="Predicted"] <-"phi"
  names(phiNB)[names(phiNB) =="Predicted"] <-"phi"
  names(abNB)[names(abNB) =="Predicted"] <-"abund"
  mrgNB<-merge (phiNB[,c(1,5,32)],abNB[,c(1,5,29,32)], by=c("plot","year"),
              all.x=T,all.y=T)
  mrg<-merge (phi[,c(1,6,14)],ab[,c(1,3:5)], by=c("plot","year"),
              all.x=T,all.y=T)
  rb <-rbind (mrgNB,mrg)
  rb$dens <- (rb$abund*rb$phi)/0.07854
  ta<-tapply(rb$dens,list(rb$year,rb$stand),mean)
  ta<-data.frame(ta)
  x <-unlist(ta, use.names = F)
}
#
set.seed(1)
(pbN <- parboot(mod, Nhat, nsim=7, report=1)) #use nsim=200 for a "real" run

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] combining predict and ranef to estimate density
parts:
hi Mike,
 in principle I think what you're doing is ok but one thing: Ranef() is not doing a bootstrap. Rather, it is computing the posterior mean and intervals by plugging in the MLE (so it is empirical Bayesian ).
 I guess it does make sense to bootstrap that, as you've done, to account for uncertainty due to having to estimate the parameters, but that is not related to the empirical Bayesianism of the whole thing.

regards
andy

parts:
Understood, Andy, thanks.  Do you see any advantage to using both predict() and ranef() as I did here, versus using only ranef()?  The main reason I've attempted to use both is because including the un-surveyed plots basically triples the number of plots and so includes more habitat heterogeneity throughout a stand.  But I'm not sure it's worth that if it makes the procedure questionable.  
 
Mike Worland

hi Mike,
 I don't know... I think you could use either one or the other but I don't see a reason to use both, is there?  I mean you could estimate N or generate predictions of E(N) but why use both?

messages.author: 0c8e4d9395a2aae5
messages.subject: Re: combining predict and ranef to estimate density
parts:
Andy, if you're wondering why then I certainly am.  I thought using both might work because I have 2 types of plots: those sampled for both habitat traits and birds, and those sampled for habitat only.  I used ranef() on the former and predict() on the later.  The 2 other alternatives I believe are to just use predict() on all plots or to just use ranef() on only the surveyed plots.  I tried all 3 approaches for Least Flycatcher with these results for 4 stands.  The dashed line at 2008 shows treatment application.
 
 

 
I made some preliminary confidence intervals and the ranef() only intervals are the widest with upper 95% limits averaging around 3x greater than lower limits.  Predict() only and the combined approach have similar confidence intervals with upper limits less than 2x greater than lower.
 
Any thoughts after seeing these results?  Predict() alone looks too manufactured and unrealistic to me.  Notice that the control and treatment 1 stands overlap perfectly.  The neater appearance of the graph for the combined approach I think is due to the influence of this unrealistic trend.  
 
It seems like my main problem is understanding the difference between ranef() and predict().  I found two other threads which were quite helpful in this regard (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/ranef$20predict/unmarked/bT6M0NbuQAM/ehhklwzJjmwJ and https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/ranef$20predict/unmarked/0G0pzyMPuoI/9KjyDvUylXAJ).  From these threads and this comparison I'm leaning towards using only ranef() despite the fuzzier results.  Does that seem reasonable?  I would really appreciate other thoughts on this.
 
Mike Worland
